asked.text:
Phase 0 goal: a working foundation that can run the agents in a simulated environment. Deliver:
1. Repo layout as in the spec (Python, uv, typed with pydantic, pytest), README with setup and architecture overview, the spec copied into docs/.
2. Data layer: DuckDB schema for the spec's data model (trades, prices, filings, observations, arguments, theses, thesis_links, predictions, anomaly_events, graph nodes/edges, guide versions, run plans, etc.) with migrations.
3. Append-only, hash-chained action log written only by the harness/tool gateway; agents get read-only access; tamper detection verify command; plan-vs-actual reconciler that flags claims not backed by log entries.
4. Tool gateway: deterministic tools exposed via MCP, every call logged, point-in-time enforcement (blocks data dated after the simulated 'as-of' date), risk-cap enforcement hooks. Start with SEC EDGAR fetch (requires User-Agent from env var), a price data adapter (pluggable; ship a free/default source such as yfinance or Stooq plus an Alpaca adapter stub reading ALPACA_API_KEY/ALPACA_SECRET_KEY env vars), ratio computation.
5. Citation model: numbers in agent output must reference tool-output IDs; validator that drops uncited claims.
6. Historical replay simulator framed as an RL-style env (observation = point-in-time state, actions = buy/sell/hold/size, multi-objective reward per spec), with costs/slippage, walk-forward splits, held-out sectors, and buy-and-hold/SPY baselines. Paper-trading runner interface for Alpaca (works when keys are present, cleanly skips otherwise).
7. Minimal Claude Agent SDK wiring: an orchestrator plus one or two simple agents (e.g. fundamentals analyst and risk manager) that run a full loop in the simulator end-to-end using the MCP tools; ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from env; if absent, a deterministic mock-LLM mode so tests and the demo still run.
8. Guide/skill versioning stubs for the GSO self-evolution loop (metaskill with the six sections, versioned guides, proposal records) — implementation of evolution can be a stub but schema and interfaces should be real.
9. Tests covering the log hash chain, point-in-time blocking, citation validator, reconciler, and a short simulator run. Make `make demo` (or equivalent) run a short offline simulation in mock mode and print a report.

The next components to build are caps, portfolio, gateway, and tools.

ToolContext is being designed as the central context object for tool execution. The build order is portfolio and costs first, then caps, then tools, then gateway. Portfolio will use a Lot dataclass to track quantity and total cost.

Portfolio is being defined with cash, positions, peak equity, friction, swing exits, holding samples, closed PnLs, an equity curve, contributions, and trades. A Fill dataclass tracks individual trade details including ticker, side, quantity, price, fees, and session. The Portfolio class also includes a market_value method to compute total value from current prices.

The half_spread pricing function is being drafted in sim/costs.py. It applies tiered spreads based on price and liquidity thresholds, then adjusts for low trading volume. A check_caps function is also being sketched.

The check_caps algorithm is being defined. It takes proposed weights, metadata, equity, peak, options premium, and day-trade orders as input. A CapResult model will return whether the allocation passes, any violations, adjusted weights, and notes. The algorithm clips individual names to their single-name caps, then scales sectors, high-risk sleeves, and penny names if they exceed limits. If the total exceeds 1, all weights are scaled proportionally.

The caps algorithm repeats twice and records violations where original weights exceeded limits. Day-trade and minimum-hold guards are order-level, not weight-level, so they will live in a separate `apply_order_guards` function. That function identifies buys by ticker across the order list, then blocks any sell orders on tickers that were just bought in the same session.

The `apply_order_guards` function now also enforces minimum hold periods. It checks the gap between the current session and the position entry session, and blocks sells that fall below the minimum hold window. Cap-reduction sells are marked with a special reason so they can be excluded from day-trade detection. The sizing logic will compare pre-cap and post-cap target weights to identify when a sell is triggered by a cap clip rather than a rebalance.

The sizing algorithm will build equal weights among selected names first, then enforce sector and sleeve caps. Any weight reduction from that step triggers a cap_reduction sell.

A drawdown halt is being added: new high-risk buys are blocked once equity falls 20% or more below peak, and a de-risk review is recommended at 30%.

An option gate function is also being drafted.

The option gate will open only when options are enabled and equity meets the minimum threshold. The sizer tool will accept a selected ticker list and read caps and rules internally, keeping all sizing math inside the tool.

The `size_position` implementation is being drafted. It computes equity from the portfolio state and incoming cash, then builds raw equal weights across the selected tickers capped by their single-name limits. Those raw weights are passed to `enforce_caps` along with metadata and risk settings. Current positions not in the selection are forced to zero weight. The function then iterates over the adjusted weights to generate orders.

The sizer tool now computes each ticker's current position value and compares it to the target weight scaled by equity. A rebalance band skips small gaps that fall below a minimum notional threshold or a percentage of equity. Buys are issued when the gap exceeds the minimum notional, while sells use a "cap_reduction" reason for tickers whose weights were clipped by caps and a "rebalance" reason otherwise.

The `size_position` tool will return orders, adjusted weights, violations, equity, and incoming cash. A rebalance band skips trades when the gap between target and current weight is small; new names start at zero so they are always traded. The `check_caps` tool will validate weights without generating orders, and the risk manager will call it after sizing. Allowed tools will be listed in `harness/permissions.py`, and `ToolContext` will live in `harness/context.py` so tools can import it without depending on the gateway.

ToolContext is being defined with fields for the current date, store, portfolio, settings, incoming cash, session index, and log directory. A registry decorator is being added to `registry.py` so tools can register themselves by name, version, description, and phase.

The registry module will define the `tool` decorator and `REGISTRY` dictionary at the top, then import tool modules at the bottom to populate the registry. Tool modules will import only the `tool` decorator from registry, avoiding a circular dependency with `REGISTRY`. A `load()` function may be added to finalize registration after all modules are imported.

The gateway `call` method will look up tools by name in the registry, validate permissions, and raise a configuration error if the tool is missing. The registry import pattern is confirmed safe: tools import the decorator at module level while the registry imports them at load time.

The gateway `call` method now handles tool execution with explicit exception branches. It raises `PermissionDenied` for blocked tools, records `LeakageAttempt` as a leakage event and increments the counter, and maps `PhaseNotImplemented` to an error status.

The gateway call method now rounds floats in tool outputs and serializes them to canonical JSON. It hashes the output and arguments to generate IDs, then logs the call before storing the result.

The gateway call method now returns a ToolResult object. Leakage and blocked exceptions propagate upward so the agent loop aborts trading. Phase-not-implemented errors return a result instead of raising, preventing catalog probes from crashing. A future-date check is being drafted to reject arguments dated after the current simulation date.

The future-date check now scans arguments for `end`, `end_date`, and `as_of` keys. It rejects any date that falls after the current simulation date.

A `prices_eod` tool is being drafted to fetch point-in-time end-of-day bars. It validates the ticker against the security store and parses the requested start and end dates.

The `prices_eod` tool now fetches point-in-time bars from the store and returns the ticker, security ID, sleeve, sector, date range, bar count, and raw bar data. Returning the full history may be excessive for ratio calculations, so the output might be trimmed to only the tail needed.

The `prices_eod` tool will return only a summary of the fetched range, including the first and last dates, last close, and last open. The full bar series is unnecessary because the ratio tool reads the store directly. This keeps the output small while still providing enough data to cite the last close.

The ratio tool will recompute metrics deterministically from the store using adjusted close, avoiding LLM reliance and keeping log size small. It will read 200 days of point-in-time prices and fundamentals to compute volatility, multi-period returns, drawdown, liquidity, valuation ratios, and a quality score.

A universe tool is being drafted to return the current security universe with ticker, security ID, sleeve, sector, and exchange.

A `guides.get_active` tool will read guide files from disk and compare their versions against `settings.guide_versions`. A `write_observation` tool will persist observations to the store and return an observation ID. The `verify.citations` tool will delegate to a pure function, and the `audit.diff` tool will call the reconciler using log entries and outputs.

The `audit.diff` tool will read prior log entries and outputs from the store and log directory, with memo text and claims passed as arguments. A `verify_chain` tool will run `LogView(ctx.log_dir).verify()` and return the status; it sees only prior entries because the current call has not yet been appended. A `broker.render_ticket` tool is being drafted to format a list of orders into ticket lines.

`broker.render_ticket` returns formatted order lines and a venue label without network access. `broker.alpaca_paper_submit` is gated to the broker agent only, so the risk manager cannot accidentally trigger paper trades; it returns skipped when keys are missing and is tested directly and through the gateway. `thesis.validate` and `thesis.write` are fully implemented. Remaining tools are left as stubs.

Phase 0 tool inventory is now complete. The real tools cover EDGAR filings, market data, risk checks, portfolio sizing, observations, guides, citations, audit diffs, logging, broker tickets, paper submission, and thesis validation. Stubs remain for EDGAR section extraction and XBRL fact retrieval.

A thin XBRL facts reader will be implemented since the underlying data exists. A lightweight corporate actions tool is also planned. DCF and peer multiples remain stubs, while the quality score stays inside compute_ratios. The screen.run tool will be a real wrapper that applies screening rules to ratio outputs, reusing the existing ratio function to avoid double math.

The scope is being narrowed to the tools the agent loop actually needs. News.fetch_events and news.classify_event will remain stubs that raise PhaseNotImplemented. The real tools are now EDGAR filings, thesis validation and writing, minimal prediction scoring, XBRL facts reading, option gating, ticket rendering, and paper submission.

Anomaly detection, graph traversal, industry transcripts, and simulation tools are being added to the real tool set. A real `verify.lookup_fact` will read prior tool outputs by ID from the database. `reopen_source` and `match_quote` remain phase two stubs. The thesis scoring logic will live in `mcp_servers/thesis_tools.py`.

A pure-function citation validator is being drafted. It uses regex to strip bracketed citations, then scans the remaining text for unquoted numbers and marks them as removed.

The citation validator is finalized. It uses regex to replace citations with spaces of identical length, preserving text spans so the uncited-number scanner can safely strip unquoted numbers from the original text. A `validate_claims` function is being drafted to iterate over claims, apply this stripping, and separate kept claims from dropped ones.

The `validate_claims` function now enforces claim integrity. It drops fact claims that lack `fact_refs` or a `log_entry_id`, and rejects any fact whose referenced output IDs are missing from the known set. Forecast claims without references are also being filtered out.

The citation validator now preserves fact claims that carry references even when unquoted numbers are stripped from the prose. A reconciler is being drafted.

The reconciler is being implemented as a `reconcile` function that returns an `AuditReport`. It defines regex patterns to extract counts of stocks analysed and filings read from log entries. It tallies successful tool calls per run ID and compares them against the plan's expected tools, flagging any tool that was called fewer times than its minimum required.

The reconciler assigns severity levels to discrepancies. Missing expected tools are marked high if they have a minimum call count of one or more, otherwise medium. Excess calls and unplanned broker tool invocations are also flagged, with broker calls carrying higher severity. The function then extracts activity counts from the memo text and prior outputs.

The reconciler now validates claim fact references. It checks that every referenced output ID exists in the prior outputs and flags a high-severity discrepancy if any reference is missing. It also verifies that the stored output JSON matches its SHA256 hash, raising a high severity alert for tampered or corrupted outputs.

The reconciler now validates the security universe size against the plan and checks guide versions against the active set. It flags a high-severity discrepancy if either check fails. The audit status is fail for any high severity, warn for any medium severity, and pass otherwise. The tool wrapper adds chain status to the output. Log entries are filtered by run_id so prior runs do not interfere with the current audit.

The citation validator will query the store for known output IDs. Claims are passed as lists of dictionaries and parsed into Claim models. Tool arguments are stored by hash only; the audit tool receives memo text and returns discrepancies without echoing the full memo.

The simulation layer will be split into three files: `src/ta/sim/portfolio.py`, `src/ta/sim/fills.py`, and `src/ta/sim/env.py`. Caps will be written as testable units that do not depend on the gateway. The `size_position` tool will insert decisions directly into the portfolio, using security IDs from the store and rule versions from settings. Position snapshots will be handled inside the environment rather than inside a tool.

DuckDB date comparisons in the universe filter and price inserts are being verified. The generate_bars shock logic was simplified to avoid an unpredictable branch, though it remains deterministic.

The simulation's random number consumption is now fully deterministic. A single market shock vector is drawn once per ticker, and each ticker's idiosyncratic shock is drawn before its loop begins. Delisted tickers simply iterate fewer times, so they consume fewer extra draws without affecting the sequence for later tickers.

A quick sanity check on the SMLL quality score shows that with earnings of 4e7, a market cap of 5e7, and a price near 12, the earnings yield calculates to roughly 6.7%.

The SMLL quality score correctly excludes PENY because its negative earnings yield is penalized below zero. Cores with positive yields are selected, and the agent caps picks at three names; XOM should consistently appear due to its high yield. JNJ was assigned a net income of 18e9 to keep its yield reasonable. The 180-day volatility lookback has sufficient history within the demo window.

The agent will request 180 days of historical prices ending on the as_of date. If a ticker was listed after that window, the query simply returns fewer bars.

The orchestrator plan expects price calls for every core and high-risk security in the universe. The agent will iterate the universe tool output and skip benchmarks to match this count exactly.

GONE was delisted before 2024, so it is excluded from the late demo window.

The demo universe contains eight tickers: six analysed plus SPY and AGG. The orchestrator plan expects one `prices_eod` and one `compute_ratios` call per security, plus a single call each for guides, portfolio state, universe lookup, observation writes, sizing, caps, option gate, ticket rendering, citations, and audit. A missing or failed price call will cause the tool count to diverge from expectations, triggering an audit failure that blocks order execution.

The agent loop will read the security universe and filter for core and high-risk tickers to build the plan. It will insert the run plan into the store before any tool calls begin. Every analysed security gets a `write_observation` entry, even if it is not selected for trading.

The agent loop is being drafted as a concrete sequence: call guides and portfolio state, query the security universe, then iterate over each analysed ticker to fetch prices, compute ratios, and write observations. After gathering all ratio results, an LLM judge evaluates them against screen rules. The loop also validates that selection fact references exist before proceeding to risk checks.

The agent loop now completes the sizing and risk phase. It calls `size_position` with the selected tickers, then validates weights against caps, checks the option gate, writes a risk observation, and renders a ticket from the resulting orders. Claims are built from the LLM judgement and ratio results, passed to the citation verifier, and then to the auditor for discrepancy review. If the audit fails or citations are rejected, the order list is cleared; otherwise execution proceeds.

The agent will filter the universe tool output to match the precomputed plan count, ensuring tool call expectations remain aligned. The orchestrator plan is generated by the harness before any tool calls begin; the orchestrator agent merely confirms it by querying portfolio state and active guides.

The orchestrator plan is deterministic code in `agents/orchestrator.py` that reads the store to build the RunPlan. A comment will note that the plan hash is stored before the logged tool calls begin. The citation verifier and audit tools are included in the same run and execute after the analyst phase, so their call counts are already reflected in the expected tool totals.

A flaw was found in the audit tool: when it runs, it counts log entries already written, but its own expected call has not yet been appended. This would cause the audit to flag itself as missing. The fix is either to exclude tail tools from the count or to set the audit call’s minimum to zero so the harness validates the returned output directly.

The reconciler will treat `audit.diff` as an in-flight tool by passing it in the `in_flight_tools` set. This lets the audit count its own expected call without a separate special case.

The reconciler will accept an `in_progress` list of tool names and count each as already present. The harness will pass `["audit.diff"]` during the audit call so its own expected entry is not flagged as missing. A second reconcile run without that list would see the stored audit result.

The in-flight tool workaround is abandoned. The plan will omit `verify.citations` and `audit.diff` from its expected tools. Those tail calls will be logged after the agent loop and flagged as unplanned MEDIUM severity.

Flagging tail tools as unplanned would produce a WARN status, which is undesirable for a clean demo. The chosen approach is to include `verify.citations`, `audit.diff`, and `log.verify_chain` in the orchestrator plan and use the `in_progress` reconciler flag so the audit tool counts its own expected call without special-case logic.

The audit tool will append its own log entry immediately upon return. The harness will then run a second reconcile without the in-flight flag to confirm counts match. If the post-check reveals discrepancies, the audit status upgrades to fail.

The harness will compute the final audit report after all tool calls complete, including audit.diff. The audit tool will run the same pure function with in_progress so its logged output matches. verify.citations is already in the log before audit.diff runs, so only audit.diff needs in-flight accounting. Claims are built before verification and passed to the verifier, which drops some and returns the kept set.

The audit tool receives a memo built from the kept claims returned by the verifier. The memo's stock count reflects the distinct securities in the ratio results. Dropped facts are excluded from the memo, so the audit checks only the retained content. Citation accuracy is judged by comparing dropped and kept fact counts.

The memo will use British spelling: "Analysed {n} stocks." The demo skips filings, so that sentence is omitted. The word "analysed" appears only once with a number. Risk observation text contains no digits.

Fact claims for weights and quality scores are rendered as FACT lines in the memo, substituting placeholders like [F-2] rather than embedding raw numbers. The option gate boolean is also cited without a bare number. This keeps the audit text free of digits that could trigger the fact stripper.

The audit tool scans the rendered memo, which displays resolved numbers next to citation IDs. The reconciler only checks activity claims and fact references, not that the memo contains zero digits. The citation validator strips uncited numbers from claim text before rendering, so bare numbers in the final output do not trigger audit failures.

The audit tool will scan the rendered memo for uncited numbers. It will ignore values immediately followed by a FactRef marker or those embedded in dates. This keeps the audit lightweight while still catching free-text numbers that lack proper citations.

The audit tool will not scan the rendered memo for uncited numbers. The citation validator strips claim prose before rendering, and the memo template uses only those claims plus structured fields. A dedicated test will cover the stripper, while the reconciler checks structured activity sentences and fact references.

The fact stripper serves as the regex/NER pass required by the spec. It runs on every claim and on any freeform opinion string before the memo is assembled. Activity claims are intentionally numeric and are verified against the log separately from fact claims, so they are not stripped.

A `strike_activity_claims` helper will replace unbacked activity claims with a placeholder when audit discrepancies reach HIGH severity. The simulation environment will use a shared `simulate_orders` function and a `Book` class to track portfolio state, mark prices, and handle contributions.

The `Book` class will track cash, contributions, and apply corporate actions like splits and delistings. Split quantities scale by ratio while cost basis stays unchanged. The simulation fixture does not include splits, so unit tests will exercise this logic on a minimal book.

Delisting will trigger a full exit at the last known close with standard sell slippage, ensuring exact test outcomes. The simulation environment's `step` method will return a `StepResult` and mark the session complete once no more trading days remain.

The `step` method advances the day index and marks prices. It contributes cash at month boundaries and applies corporate actions. Orders are filtered, filled, and trades recorded. Portfolio equity is updated before advancing to the next day.

The simulation environment will set the gateway's as-of date to the current day after each step so subsequent decisions reflect the latest state. Observations will use the latest bar for each security rather than execution bars. Incoming cash is computed as the monthly contribution only when a new month begins. A `decision_due` method will determine whether the agent should submit orders at the current step.

The gateway as-of date is set from the environment at each decision. The equity curve records initial cash before any step. Baselines reuse the same date loop and fill logic but use their own Book and skip the gateway. They see only current prices via prices_asof. A simple SPY buy-and-hold baseline needs no ratio data.

The baseline policy will receive the incoming cash amount as a parameter. Because the simulation environment applies monthly contributions before executing orders inside each step, the policy must account for that cash when computing order notional. This ensures the baseline invests the full available balance rather than leaving it idle until the next decision.

The agent sizer will also receive the incoming cash amount in its context. On the first trading day, the policy buys roughly one thousand dollars of SPY because no contribution is due yet. When a month boundary arrives, the sizer includes the incoming contribution before the step adds it and fills the order.

The equal-weight baseline will allocate each security a 1/n fraction of total equity plus incoming cash. It computes a target value for each holding and only submits buy orders to reach that target, never selling unless a delisting forces an exit.

The baseline policies will use a simple buy-and-hold strategy with monthly contribution top-ups. Underweight holdings receive new cash, while overweight positions remain untouched. A 60/40 SPY and AGG split is also planned. A rules-only baseline will select names with positive earnings yield from core or high-risk sleeves, equal-weight them, cap allocations, and rebalance without the agent’s max_names limit or volatility penalty.

A shared `compute_ratio_block` helper in fund.py will let baselines compute earnings yield directly without gateway side effects. The Book will track friction and swing. A pure metrics module will derive reward from equity curve data, contributions, audit statistics, and weights.

A pure walk-forward split helper will be added to splits.py. A paper broker module is planned for sim/paper.py before building the agents, memo, CLI, tests, and README.

DuckDB schema migrations will be excluded from table name checks. Duplicate insert guards are already in place for sync operations. The demo wipes the database before seeding fresh data. Tests use isolated databases to avoid unique constraint violations.

An `analysed_names` helper will centralize the logic for retrieving names that have been analyzed.

The `is_analysed` helper will live in `ta/data/universe.py` so agents avoid fixture imports. The gateway needs a `set_as_of` method, and the portfolio must be created before the gateway and shared between them.

The fill math is being refined to prevent negative cash. A buy order is rejected if the notional is below the minimum or the open price is non-positive. The filled quantity is computed from the available cash budget, accounting for slippage and commission per share, then rounded to six decimals.

Buy fills are clamped to the available cash budget so the book never goes negative. Sell fills are capped at the held quantity and use a discounted price for slippage plus per-share commission.

Sell fills update the book’s cash balance and record closed PnL. The position is fully exited if the sold quantity matches the held lot, or partially reduced otherwise. A day-trade guard runs before every fill, and the environment rechecks weight caps after orders are submitted to drop any noncompliant buys.

The environment will implement `orders_respect_caps` to enforce weight limits. Peak equity will be tracked on every mark so drawdown can be computed from the equity curve. A high-risk buy halt will drop those orders when equity falls within a threshold of its peak. The order filter will carry sleeve information and live in `caps.py` as `guard_orders`. A `_std` helper is being added for volatility calculations.

A `_std` helper will compute sample standard deviation from a list of numbers. Returns will be derived as log differences between consecutive adjusted closes. Max drawdown will be measured over the last 63 trading days. The output will include a `fundamentals_available_at` timestamp to indicate when ratio inputs are available. The MCP server will be implemented after inspecting the mcp package API, likely using FastMCP's `add_tool`.

The MCP server will use FastMCP 1.9+ dynamic registration. A `@mcp.tool()` decorator and `add_tool` method will expose the gateway tools. The server will be named "ta-gateway".

The MCP server will register tools by wrapping each spec and replacing dots with underscores in tool names. The wrapper reads environment variables such as TA_DB, TA_LOG_DIR, and TA_AS_OF because the stdio server runs as a separate process. Phase 0 uses an in-process gateway as the authoritative source of truth. A subprocess MCP server cannot share the simulation’s portfolio state in memory.

The SDK will be checked for in-process MCP support. If the package exposes a dict of callables, the gateway will run inside the simulation process. Otherwise the subprocess MCP server will answer data queries against the shared DuckDB file, but portfolio state must be passed in the prompt because the subprocess cannot hold the Book. This limitation will be documented honestly.

An `agents/sdk.py` module will wrap the in-process gateway for the Claude Agent SDK. It imports `tool` and `create_sdk_mcp_server`, then builds a list of tools that close over the shared gateway instance. If the SDK is unavailable, it returns None.

If the Claude Agent SDK is missing, the code will raise a ConfigError with install instructions. The `make_tool` wrapper will be written against the documented decorator, and tests can mock it without requiring the extra to be installed. A small stdio MCP entry point will also be added so data tools can run as a standalone process using environment variables.

A lightweight in-process test helper will invoke gateway tools directly by name and arguments, bypassing stdio entirely. The MCP server itself is the FastMCP wrapper. Tests will verify that the registry keys match the expected tool names and that `build_server()` returns a valid object with tools attached.

The beta shock formula is being simplified to avoid a numpy bug. The 80-day delisting window is confirmed feasible given roughly 370 business days of history. A manual portfolio test for corporate splits will be added, separate from the fixture-based tests.

A new `apply_actions` method will be added to the portfolio book to process corporate actions such as splits. It will accept an `id_to_ticker` resolver because actions are keyed by security ID while positions are keyed by ticker. Delisting events will sell held shares at the previous close price, since no bar exists on the delist date.

The universe module will drop a name from the active set on its delist date. A focused unit test will buy a GONE security before its 80-day delisting window and step across the ex-date to verify liquidation. The environment must run for at least 81 steps to cover that gap.

The test will use manual orders instead of the agent to buy GONE on day zero, then step through the 81-day delisting window with empty orders to hold the position. DuckDB queries are fast enough for this approach.

The delisting test will verify that GONE is absent from the portfolio after the 80-day window. The liquidation logic must run before fills on the ex-date, and it will bypass minimum-hold rules because delisting is mandatory. The README will be written only after tests pass so it can reference real commands.

The gateway will use canonical JSON serialization for date arguments. OrderIntent objects will be converted to dictionaries via model_dump. If an audit check fails, the agent returns empty orders but the simulation still records the audit and holds the position.

A `harness/caps.py` module will hold pure weight-enforcement functions. The `name_cap` helper will return the high-risk percentage for high-risk or penny-price names, and the core percentage otherwise. Episode-level rule compliance will count any order drops that the guard orders step makes.

Any core name priced below the penny threshold will be treated as a penny security and counted toward the 10% penny total cap, regardless of its sleeve. Sector caps will group positions by sector and scale any group that exceeds its percentage limit.

An `in_high_risk_sleeve` helper will flag any security priced below the penny threshold as high-risk, so small, micro, speculative, and penny names all count toward the 30% high-risk sleeve cap. Options premiums are zero in phase 0. The `enforce` algorithm normalizes weights to non-negative floats and collects violations.

The enforcement loop iterates up to four times. Each pass clips individual ticker weights to their single-name cap and records violations. After that, weights are grouped by sector and any sector total exceeding its cap is flagged.

Sector and high-risk sleeve caps are scaled by the ratio of the allowed percentage to the current total weight. The algorithm then computes the penny total across all names priced below the threshold.

The enforcement loop now scales the penny total cap and normalizes all weights to sum to one. Violations are deduplicated by ticker and name so that only the original excess is recorded, even if multiple iterations trigger the same cap.

The `ok` flag is set to False whenever the original weights already violate a cap, ensuring adjusted weights must pass a second validation. Concrete test cases are being designed to exercise each enforcement layer: a single core name at 50% will be clipped to 15%, two tech names at 20% each will trigger sector scaling, and seven high-risk names at 5% each will exceed the 30% sleeve limit.

Unit tests will use fake metadata because the fixture only contains two high-risk names. A day-trade test will drop a sell order when its ticker is also bought in the same order list. Minimum-hold logic will reject rebalance exits that fall short of the required session count, but cap-reduction exits are allowed. The guard_orders implementation will enforce these rules. Swing exits will be tracked per calendar quarter; if a security is held for fewer than the required swing sessions and the current quarter already has too many swings, the exit is blocked.

Partial rebalance trims are not counted as swing trades and do not increment the swing counter or trigger the swing cap. Only full discretionary exits qualify as swings. A partial trim of a position younger than the minimum hold period will still be blocked by the minimum-hold rule.

The first rebalance at session 5 is allowed because the position has reached the minimum hold of 5 sessions. Entry session is defined as the fill date index, so a fill on step 1 sets entry_session to 1.

Cash weight is implicitly set to one minus the sum of all security weights, so it is never constrained by caps. The guard_orders step will use the upcoming fill session as current index plus one.

Weight outputs will be rounded to six decimals to prevent tiny float noise from triggering churn. The rebalance band is set to 0.01. Notional amounts and limit prices are rounded to two decimals for ticket formatting. Simulated fills execute at the open rather than at the limit price.
